name: Buddha-nature in Chan, Seon and Zen

definitions.definition: The nature of awakening in every being, identical with the self-nature; 'if the self-nature is awakened, beings are buddhas; if deluded, buddhas are beings'.
'Whole being is buddha-nature'; impermanence is buddha-nature (Dōgen).
'All beings are originally buddhas' like ice and water (Hakuin).
One's own numinous knowing is the true buddha (Jinul).

relations.note: Chan inherits the Nirvāṇa-sūtra and Awakening of Faith teaching; the embryo image is rare in Chan.

definitions.definition: The self-nature is originally pure, unborn, complete, unmoving and productive of all dharmas; delusion only covers it like clouds cover the sky.
Buddhas and beings are only the one mind, without beginning or end, beyond all measure (Huangbo).
The one mind as the source that mirrors the myriad dharmas (Yanshou).

relations.note: Chan's one mind draws on Laṅkāvatāra and Awakening of Faith language; not identical with Yogācāra's analysis of consciousness.

name: The true person of no rank

definitions.definition: The one listening to the Dharma here and now, going in and out of the senses, dependent on nothing, yet not to be reified.

relations.note: Linji's 'true person' is not a soul that leaves the body; he calls it a 'dried shit-stick' to prevent reification.

name: The 'Śreṇika heresy' (eternal mind-nature in a perishing body)

definitions.definition: The view, reported of certain southern teachers, that the knowing nature is permanent and leaves the perishing body at death; Nanyang Huizhong equates it with the heretic Śreṇika.
Dōgen rejects it: body and mind are one, nature and form not two.

relations.note: Chan distinguishes buddha-nature from an eternal self.

names.name: fushō no busshin 不生の仏心

definitions.definition: The buddha-mind is unborn and marvellously illuminating; everything is resolved in it without striving (Bankei).
One's face before thinking good or evil; the self-nature pointed to directly.
The empty, calm, numinous knowing mind (Jinul).
The unobscured knowing of the empty, quiescent mind — the true nature; 'the one word knowing is the gate of all wonders'.
Recognised by tracing back the radiance: the one who hears, sees and asks.

relations.note: Both describe a knowing nature of mind not obscured by defilements; the Chan term derives from Zongmi/Heze, not from the Pali luminous-mind passage; Theravāda does not treat the luminous citta as an ultimate.

name: No-thought as tenet, no-form as substance, non-abiding as root

definitions.definition: The Platform Sūtra's three: no-thought is not being stained by objects amid thought (not blankness), no-form is being free of forms amid forms, non-abiding is the original nature that does not stop in any dharma.
No-thought as tenet (Shenhui).
No-thought alone as the whole of practice (Wuzhu).
Being without the mind of seeking and discriminating is the ultimate; 'one person of the Way without mind' surpasses offerings to all buddhas (Huangbo).
Ten ways of practising no-mind (Jinsim jikseol).
Samādhi is the substance of prajñā and prajñā the function of samādhi, like a lamp and its light.
Calm yet always knowing, knowing yet always calm — the content of cultivation after awakening.

relations.note: Chan's dinghui corresponds to calm and insight but denies their sequence ('do not say samādhi first produces prajñā').

name: Balance of alertness and calm (xingxing jiji)

definitions.definition: Calm without alertness is dullness; alertness without calm is scattered thought (Yongjia).
If illumination loses silence there is aggression; if silence loses illumination, murkiness (Hongzhi).
Jinul's seongjeok deungji; sequential counteraction is the gradual method.
Silence in which words are forgotten and clarity appears; silence and illumination complete each other (Hongzhi).
Criticised by Dahui as 'heretical silent-illumination Chan' that turns practitioners into dead ash.

name: Sudden and gradual (dun / jian)

definitions.definition: The Dharma has no sudden or gradual; people are sharp or dull; the deluded cultivate gradually, the awakened accord suddenly (Platform Sūtra); Shenxiu's verse is presented as gradual, Huineng's as sudden.
Sudden awakening followed by gradual cultivation (Shenhui as read by Zongmi).
Sudden awakening to principle with gradual removal of habit energies (Guishan).
Sudden awakening, gradual cultivation as the path of all sages (Jinul); contested by Seongcheol.

relations.note: The Indian/Pali gradual training is one of the positions the sudden teaching relativises.

notes: Debate owned by U50 as dsp:sudden-or-gradual; this concept records the Chan formulations.

definitions.definition: Seeing one's own nature at the words; examples: Huineng on the Diamond Sūtra, Xiangyan at the pebble, Lingyun at peach blossoms, Dongshan at his reflection.
The breakthrough of great doubt (Hakuin at the temple bell), to be followed by post-awakening practice.
Awakening is like the moon in water; Dōgen de-emphasises kenshō as a goal separate from practice.

relations.note: Corresponds to the path of seeing (darśanamārga) of the five paths; band B5 (first direct seeing) in the interpretation layer.

definitions.definition: The mass of doubt raised with the whole body on the huatou; 'great doubt, great awakening'.
Hakuin's great doubt 'as if frozen in a sheet of ice' before the breakthrough.
Bankei (in the Rinzai line) rejects cultivating doubt, saying it trades the buddha-mind for a doubt.
Great faith, great doubt, great determination (Gaofeng).
Taught in the Seon'ga gwigam.
Old cases used for commentary, verse and contemplation; the Wumen guan, Blue Cliff Record and Book of Equanimity collect them.
Dahui's contemplation of the critical phrase of a case, with the doubt kept alive in daily life.
A graded kōan curriculum under a teacher (Hakuin's line).
Dōgen collected and commented on kōans but taught just sitting; the realized kōan (genjōkōan) is reality itself.

name: Mind-to-mind transmission

definitions.definition: The Dharma is transmitted from mind to mind, each awakening himself; the robe is only a token (Hongren); the Platform Sūtra lists the line of transmission; in the Dunhuang version, possession of the text marks transmission.
The silent transmission concerned only 'knowing' (Zongmi).
Face-to-face transmission (menju) and documents of succession (shisho).

notes: The tradition's account; scholars regard the early lineage claims as constructed in the 8th century.

name: The four-line self-description of Chan

definitions.definition: 'A special transmission outside the teachings; not established on words and letters; pointing directly at the human mind; seeing the nature and becoming a buddha' — attributed to Bodhidharma.

notes: Tradition's account: Bodhidharma's teaching. Scholarly account: the phrases occur separately in Tang–Song texts; the full set is first attested in the Zuting shiyuan (1108).

name: The flower sermon

definitions.definition: On Vulture Peak the Buddha held up a flower, Mahākāśyapa smiled, and the Buddha entrusted him with the treasury of the true Dharma eye outside the teachings.

notes: Tradition's account; attested only in Chinese sources from the Song (Tiansheng guangdeng lu, 1036; the apocryphal Dafan tianwang wenfo jueyi jing).

name: The twenty-eight Indian patriarchs and six Chinese patriarchs

definitions.definition: The line from Mahākāśyapa to Bodhidharma (28) and from Bodhidharma to Huineng (six Chinese patriarchs), as listed in the Platform Sūtra and Jingde chuandeng lu; the Dunhuang Platform Sūtra gives a different list counting Huineng as 40th from the seven buddhas.

members: — Chinese: Bodhidharma, Huike, Sengcan, Daoxin, Hongren, Huineng
notes: Tradition's account. Scholarly: the 28-list was fixed in the Baolin zhuan (801); earlier lists (Fu fazang yinyuan zhuan) end with Siṃha.

name: The robe and bowl as tokens of transmission

definitions.definition: Bodhidharma's robe was handed down as a token of faith; Hongren tells Huineng not to pass it on because it causes strife; the Dunhuang version says the robe should not be transmitted.
The Baotang claim that the robe passed via Empress Wu to Zhishen and Wuzhu.
Awakening must be confirmed by a teacher; awakening without a teacher is 'natural heterodoxy' (Xuance to Yongjia).
Inka shōmei, the certification of completed training.

name: The verse contest at Huangmei

definitions.definition: Hongren asks for verses to choose his successor; Shenxiu's 'wipe the mirror' verse and Huineng's 'originally not a single thing' (Zongbao) or 'buddha-nature is always pure' (Dunhuang).

notes: Tradition's account; scholars regard the episode as a Southern-school composition.

definitions.definition: Guiyang, Linji, Caodong, Yunmen and Fayan — the lineages recognised by the Song, each with its teaching devices (Rentian yanmu).
The four classifications, four guest-host relations, four illumination-function relations, three mysteries and three essentials, and the four shouts.

Five relations of the real and the apparent (lord and minister): apparent within real, real within apparent, coming from within the real, arriving within both, arrived within both; also the five ranks of merit.
Studied as a late stage of Hakuin's kōan curriculum.

name: Principle and phenomena in Chan (li / shi, huihu)

definitions.definition: Grasping phenomena is delusion, merging with principle is not yet awakening; light and dark interfuse like the steps of walking (Cantongqi).

relations.note: Caodong language of interfusion parallels Huayan's li–shi interpenetration (U54).

definitions.definition: The mind without contrivance, grasping or rejecting, in walking, standing, sitting and lying (Mazu, Nanquan).
Just be ordinary with nothing to do (Linji).
'Supernatural power and wondrous function: carrying water and hauling firewood' (Layman Pang).
'Wash your bowl' (Zhaozhou); 'walking too is Chan' (Yongjia).
Practice amid activity surpasses practice in stillness (Hakuin).
'Cultivation and realisation are not lacking, but it cannot be defiled' (Huairang); polishing a tile does not make a mirror.
Practice and realization are one; the beginner's practice is the whole of original realization (Dōgen).
Stepping forward from the top of the hundred-foot pole.
Removing habit energies after sudden awakening.
Gogo no shugyō: Hakuin after Shōju's rebuke; Tōrei's stages.
Kuoan's ten pictures from searching for the ox to entering the marketplace.
Puming's whitening-ox series ending in 'both vanished'.
Not attaching to mind or purity, not immobility; 'sitting' is non-arising of thought toward objects, 'meditation' seeing the unmoving nature; there is no time not in samādhi.
Zazen is not learning meditation but the Dharma gate of ease and joy.
Entry by principle through faith in the one true nature and wall-gazing; entry by practice through the four practices.
Guarding the original true mind (Hongren) and guarding the one (Daoxin).
The mind that is sought cannot be found — and so is pacified (Bodhidharma and Huike).
The buddha-dharma is non-dual; the supreme Way only dislikes picking and choosing; 'faith in mind is non-dual'.
Huineng's teaching method: answer every question with its opposite so that both extremes are left behind.
Chan is 'not established on words and letters', yet the Platform Sūtra warns that saying 'no words' is itself words; reciting sūtras without understanding makes them enemies of meaning.
'Lettered Chan': literary expression is not opposed to awakening (Juefan Huihong).
Words are vehicles of the Way; one must not seek the meaning in the phrase (Yuanwu).

name: The sword that kills and the sword that gives life

definitions.definition: The teacher's double function of cutting off and restoring (Yuanwu).

name: 'If you meet the Buddha, kill the Buddha'

definitions.definition: Not being bound by any object of veneration or attachment, inner or outer; figurative, as Linji says he only cures sickness and unties bonds.
Repeated as the fruit of passing the barrier of 'wu' (Wumen).
Illness from excessive or unbalanced striving — rising heat, cold legs, fear, exhaustion — cured by naikan and the soft-butter method (Hakuin, Yasenkanna).
Wrong ways of sitting are called a 'sickness, not meditation' (Platform Sūtra); confused thought and dullness are sicknesses (Yongjia).

name: The tanden (cinnabar field) in Zen practice

definitions.definition: The lower abdomen below the navel, where breath and energy are gathered in naikan; contemplated as one's original face and Pure Land (Hakuin).
Chan generally locates the ultimate in the mind, not in a subtle body; the Platform Sūtra treats the body as a city whose king is the nature.

notes: Chan texts have no system of channels and centres comparable to haṭha or tantra; Hakuin's tanden draws on Chinese medical and Daoist language.

name: The three bodies in one's own nature

definitions.definition: Dharma, reward and transformation bodies are found in one's own nature (Platform Sūtra).
The three bodies as three lights of one's single thought (Linji).

relations.note: The trikāya read from the standpoint of the self-nature.

definitions.definition: The formless precepts, repentance and refuges given at the Dafan temple; 'when the mind is level, what need to keep precepts?'; Huineng's refraining from meat among hunters.
Eisai: the precepts are the foundation of Zen, against the Daruma school.
Receiving the precepts (jukai) and leaving home are essential (Dōgen's twelve-fascicle essays); the sixteen bodhisattva precepts.

name: The pure rules (qinggui) of Chan monasteries

definitions.definition: Baizhang's founding of separate Chan monasteries with Dharma hall, Sangha hall and communal labour; later codes (1103, 1338).
One can practise at home as well as in a monastery (Platform Sūtra); the formless verse for laypeople.
Dahui's letters teach officials to practise the huatou amid affairs.
Suzuki Shōsan: each occupation is buddha-practice.
Building temples and giving produce blessings; merit lies in the Dharma body — seeing the nature (Huineng on Emperor Wu).

name: Cause and effect for the awakened

definitions.definition: The fox kōan: 'not falling into' cause and effect brought five hundred fox-lives; 'not obscuring' cause and effect freed him.
Dōgen: deep faith in cause and effect; denial of causality is wrong view.

name: The great matter of birth and death

definitions.definition: Birth and death is the great matter, impermanence swift; merit cannot save the deluded self-nature.

name: The Pure Land as the purified mind

definitions.definition: The Western Land is near for the wise: as the mind is pure the buddha-land is pure; bodhisattvas and realms are states of mind.
'This very place is the Lotus Land' (Hakuin).

notes: Pure Land schools (U43) hold a different view of Amitābha's land; see also Ōbaku nenbutsu Zen.

definitions.definition: Time is being and being is time; each thing abides in its dharma-position; firewood does not become ash.
Reality presencing as the fundamental case: to study the self is to forget the self and be verified by the myriad dharmas.
Nanyang Huizhong: the insentient preach; one hears when free of the feelings of consciousness; Dongshan's inquiry into this led to his awakening.
Supernatural power is carrying water and hauling firewood (Layman Pang).
Powers appear only through gradual cultivation, are 'uncanny matters' and should not be used (Jinul).
Freedom in the 'samādhi of sporting in supernatural powers' belongs to one who sees the nature (Platform Sūtra).
Huineng forbids worldly mourning, leaves a last verse and dies seated; at death one should see the aggregates as empty and neither follow welcoming buddhas nor fear terrifying signs (Huangbo).
Birth-and-death is the life of the buddha (Dōgen, Shōji).
Those who cannot awaken themselves need a great good friend to show them the nature; yet each must awaken himself ('when deluded the teacher ferries, when awakened one ferries oneself').
Bodhidharma gave Huike the four-fascicle Laṅkāvatāra; Huike's followers carried it as the essence of mind; the Lengqie shizi ji builds a lineage of its masters.

name: The four wisdoms in the Platform Sūtra

definitions.definition: The eight consciousnesses are transformed into the four wisdoms — great perfect mirror, equality, wondrous observing, accomplishing what is to be done — which are 'only names without real nature', not apart from the three bodies of one's nature.

members: wisdom accomplishing what is to be done (kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna)

relations.note: Yogācāra's four wisdoms read as aspects of the self-nature.

definitions.definition: Exchanges in which the teacher responds to questions with ordinary words, gestures, shouts or blows to provoke awakening (Mazu, Linji).
Testing students for the three leaks.
Earth, water, fire and wind each return to their own nature; with the senses and their objects they branch from one root (Cantongqi).
At death, see that the four elements are without self (Huangbo).
The deluded take the four elements as their body (Jinul).
'When the four elements scatter, where do you go?' (Doushuai's third barrier).

relations.note: The Indian mahābhūtas (earth, water, fire, wind) as received in Chinese Buddhism.
